solutions.check: bars rebuilt from the blog's numbered answers (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Unglazed pottery, —— tea dish? This is baked possibly

indicators.note: 'possibly' says the letters before it could be arranged some other way

blocks.note: the whole phrase is the fodder
these letters, written after the dash, are what the shuffled phrase holds besides the answer

explanation.surface: A potter's catalogue lists an unglazed piece, wondering if it is a tea dish that was baked.
explanation.walkthrough: A composite anagram: the dash stands for the answer, and the answer plus TEA DISH is a rearrangement of THIS IS BAKED. Take away TEA DISH and four letters remain.
explanation.definitionFit: BISK is a variant spelling of bisque, the potters' term for fired but unglazed ware, also called biscuit.

clue.text: School book with something to read about antelope

indicators.note: 'about' means around, so the reading matter encloses what comes before

blocks.note: SCH is the abbreviation for school
B is the abbreviation for book
a book is something to read

explanation.surface: A school textbook about African antelope.
explanation.walkthrough: 'School book' looks like one item, but both words are abbreviated and wrapped in a second, unabbreviated book.
explanation.definitionFit: The boschbok, or bushbuck, is a small striped African antelope.

clue.text: Antique bronze, perhaps, with gold touches, put up

indicators.note: in a down entry, putting something up means writing it from the bottom to the top

blocks.note: Au is the chemical symbol for gold
to tat is to touch or pat lightly

explanation.surface: An old bronze piece with gilded highlights is put on display.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Antique' does double work: statua is an archaic form of statue, and a bronze is one example, hence 'perhaps'.
explanation.definitionFit: Statua is an old word for a statue, and a bronze is a cast statue.

clue.text: Two jackdaws and a parrot

blocks.note: ka, also spelt kae, is a Scots word for a jackdaw
the second of the two

explanation.surface: A birdwatcher's tally: two jackdaws and a parrot.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Two' tells you to write the Scots jackdaw word twice.
explanation.definitionFit: The kaka is a large olive-brown New Zealand parrot.

clue.text: Measure (formerly) to diffuse substance (8, three words)

blocks.note: an en is a printer's unit of measure
sperse is an obsolete Spenserian verb meaning to disperse

explanation.surface: An old recipe for spreading some substance thinly by measured amounts.
explanation.walkthrough: The answer is a Latin phrase; '(formerly)' marks the archaic verb.
explanation.definitionFit: Ens per se is the philosophers' term for an entity existing in itself, that is, a substance.

clue.text: Edible fungus, all right in wine (not weak) coming up

indicators.note: 'in' puts the approval word inside the drink
weak is abbreviated W, so 'not weak' removes that letter
in a down entry, coming up means reading from bottom to top

blocks.note: taken as written
OK means all right

explanation.surface: A mushroom recipe: the fungus is fine cooked in wine, as long as it is not a weak one.
explanation.walkthrough: Drop W, turn what is left of the wine upside down, and set OK in its middle.
explanation.definitionFit: Enoki are long thin white mushrooms much used in Japanese cooking.

clue.text: Former standards having to kick in for very old-fashioned fusspot

indicators.note: 'in' places the kick inside the standards

blocks.note: a square was a Shakespearean word for a standard or rule
to toe a ball is to kick it with the toe

explanation.surface: Old rules are thrown out to make way for a stuffy, fussy person.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Former' marks the old sense of square; 'having to kick in' reads like being obliged to contribute.
explanation.definitionFit: Square-toes is an old-fashioned name for a prim, formal person, after the square-toed shoes of an earlier age.

clue.text: A couple of knaves getting on top of one in nasty spots

blocks.note: pur is an old name for the knave or jack in card games such as post and pair
the second of the pair
a means one

explanation.surface: Two rogues gang up on one person in an unpleasant place.
explanation.walkthrough: 'getting on top of' works because this is a down entry: the knaves sit above the A.
explanation.definitionFit: Purpura is a condition in which small purple spots appear on the skin from bleeding beneath it.

clue.text: Completely clean rupee, one of them crumpled

indicators.note: a crumpled note is crushed out of shape, so its letters are mixed up

blocks.note: taken as written
R is the abbreviation for one rupee

explanation.surface: Laundering a rupee note, one that had got crumpled.
explanation.definitionFit: Repure is an old verb meaning to purify thoroughly, so to make wholly clean.

clue.text: What makes it impossible to straighten coils is so awkward

definitions.text: What makes it impossible to straighten

indicators.note: something awkward is twisted or ungainly, so the letters are put in a new order

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Untangling coiled wire proves impossible because it is so awkward.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition never names the spine, which is the 'it' that cannot be straightened.
explanation.definitionFit: Scoliosis is a sideways curvature of the spine, a condition that keeps the back from being straight.

clue.text: Well imbued, after exchange of parts

indicators.note: exchanging the parts swaps the front half with the back half

blocks.note: cloth imbued with colour has been dyed

explanation.surface: A well that has become steeped in something once its parts are swapped.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Well' is a verb here: water that wells swirls up.
explanation.definitionFit: To eddy is to swirl or well up in a circular motion, as water does.

clue.text: Hybrid fruit, quaint when cooked in seaweed

indicators.note: cooking changes what goes into the pot, so the word before is remade
'in' places the cooked letters within the following word

blocks.note: taken as written
ore is an old word for seaweed, also called ware

explanation.surface: A cook adds an unusual fruit to a seaweed dish.
explanation.walkthrough: The seaweed is the dictionary word ore, not kelp or wrack; the rearranged letters go between its second and third letters.
explanation.definitionFit: The ortanique is a Jamaican citrus cross between an orange and a tangerine.

clue.text: Plumed caps tremble endlessly — likewise back to front

indicators.note: 'endlessly' tells you to drop the final letter of the word it follows
turning something back to front reads it from the other end

blocks.note: to shake is to tremble
so can mean likewise, as in 'so do I'

explanation.surface: Soldiers' feathered hats quiver in the wind.
explanation.definitionFit: A shako is a tall stiff military hat, often topped with a plume or pompom.

clue.text: Elpees bursting with 'vita', showing what enables conductor to connect (10, two words)

indicators.note: something bursting is broken apart, so its letters scatter and regroup

blocks.note: taken as written; elpees are LP records
taken as written

explanation.surface: Record sleeves crammed with life story notes, revealing what lets a musical director link up.
explanation.walkthrough: The conductor is not an orchestra's leader but a plant's food-carrying tissue.
explanation.definitionFit: In phloem, a sieve plate is the perforated wall joining one sieve tube cell to the next so sap can flow.

clue.text: Abdominal appendage getting screwed up with door

indicators.note: something screwed is twisted out of shape, so the letters are reordered

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone's injured abdomen got caught in a door.
explanation.walkthrough: 'screwed up' looks like a single phrase, but 'up' is part of the fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: A uropod is a limb on the last abdominal segment of a crustacean, forming part of the tail fan.

clue.text: Girl with work among ladies is missing lively dance

indicators.note: something among others sits inside the group
the letters of 'is' go missing from the word they are in

blocks.note: gal is a casual word for a girl
op is short for opus, a work
taken as written

explanation.surface: A girl with a job among the ladies leaves out a lively dance.
explanation.walkthrough: Strip IS from the ladies, then set the work after the first letter of what remains.
explanation.definitionFit: The gallopade, or galop, is a quick nineteenth-century ballroom dance in two-four time.

clue.text: Old, you'll lose love twice, sadly, at the proper time

indicators.note: love is zero in tennis, a round letter, and losing it twice removes two of them
'sadly' suggests things going badly, so what is left is put in a new order

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A gloomy prophecy to an old person about losing two loved ones, though only when their time comes.
explanation.walkthrough: The 'll of you'll is just 'will' joining the fodder to the instructions; take both Os from the two words and rearrange the rest.
explanation.definitionFit: Duly means properly or as expected, including at the expected or proper time.

clue.text: Henry and Laurie in transport? Lorry's more his thing!

indicators.note: being in transport means carried away in ecstasy, so the name is jumbled

blocks.note: H is the symbol for the henry, the unit of inductance
taken as written

explanation.surface: Henry and Laurie arrive by some vehicle; a lorry would suit him better.
explanation.walkthrough: 'transport' pretends to be about vehicles, and the definition plays on the same picture.
explanation.definitionFit: A haulier is a person or firm whose business is carrying goods by road, so lorries are his trade.

clue.text: Language type presenting imperial monarch in capitals

indicators.note: 'in' puts the monarch inside the abbreviation that follows

blocks.note: UC is the printers' abbreviation for upper case, that is, capital letters
GRI, Georgius Rex Imperator, was the cipher of a king who was also emperor of India

explanation.surface: A linguist names a family of languages, writing the emperor's title in block letters.
explanation.walkthrough: GRI stands for George, King and Emperor, as stamped on British coins and pillar boxes before 1947.
explanation.definitionFit: Ugric is the branch of the Finno-Ugric languages that includes Hungarian, so it names a type of language.

clue.text: Calcium modified salty earth, influence in chemical make-up

indicators.note: a modified thing has been altered, so the word after it is rearranged

blocks.note: Ca is the chemical symbol for calcium
taken as written
E is an abbreviation for earth, as on electrical plugs

explanation.surface: A chemist adds calcium to salty soil to change its composition.
explanation.definitionFit: To catalyse is to speed up a chemical reaction without being used up, so to influence a chemical change.

clue.text: Loss of concentration spoilt serve — it's lacking in terminal matches (10, two words)

indicators.note: a spoilt thing is ruined and no longer in its proper form, so the letters are rearranged

blocks.note: a blank is a moment when the mind empties
taken as written

explanation.surface: A tennis player's mind wanders and the serve goes wrong, lacking anything in the final matches.
explanation.walkthrough: 'terminal matches' sounds like the last games of a tournament, but it means rhymes, the matching sounds at line ends.
explanation.definitionFit: Blank verse is unrhymed poetry, typically iambic pentameter, so its line endings do not chime.

clue.text: Parliament head in woolly tangle in Holyrood?

indicators.note: 'in' puts the headland inside the tangled wool

blocks.note: a ness is a headland, as in Loch Ness's neighbours Fife Ness and Buchan Ness
ket is Scots for matted wool; Holyrood is the seat of the Scottish Parliament, so it hints at Scots

explanation.surface: Scottish parliament business is in a woolly tangle.
explanation.walkthrough: Holyrood, the Scottish Parliament, primes a Scottish answer, but it only signals a Scots word in the wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: The Knesset is the single-chamber parliament of Israel, sitting in Jerusalem.

clue.text: Economic theorist, one set on penetrating dimness

indicators.note: what penetrates goes inside, so these letters sit within the next word

blocks.note: taken as written
to tar on is an old phrase for to incite or set on, as a dog
mist makes everything dim

explanation.surface: An economist set on seeing through the fog of the markets.
explanation.walkthrough: 'set on' reads as 'determined', but it is the old verb meaning to urge a dog to attack.
explanation.definitionFit: A monetarist holds that controlling the money supply is the key to managing an economy.

clue.text: Dwelling hut, place going up to house friend overseas

indicators.note: in a down entry, going up means reading from the bottom to the top
to house something is to hold it inside

blocks.note: Chambers gives aim as an old verb meaning to place
ami is French for friend

explanation.surface: A simple hut goes up to give shelter to a visiting friend from abroad.
explanation.walkthrough: 'overseas' marks a foreign word, here French.
explanation.definitionFit: A mia-mia is an Australian Aboriginal shelter of branches and bark, a hut to live in.

clue.text: Appendage to mitre one's donned almost without cuts

indicators.note: almost all means one short, so the last letter of the phrase goes

blocks.note: a text given without cuts is given in full
a means one

explanation.surface: A bishop puts on his headgear, nearly uncut.
explanation.walkthrough: 'one's donned' reads as wearing, but it says the A is put on at the end.
explanation.definitionFit: An infula is one of the two ribbons hanging from the back of a bishop's mitre.

clue.text: Dialect spreading more widely, nothing accepted by lowing herd

indicators.note: what is accepted is taken in, so this letter goes inside the herd

blocks.note: O is zero, nothing
kine is the old plural of cow, and cows low

explanation.surface: A farmer notes that a regional way of speaking is spreading, while the cattle accept nothing new.
explanation.definitionFit: A koine is a dialect that spreads beyond its region to become a common tongue, like the Greek of the Hellenistic world.

clue.text: Nothing in ruins of Napoli revealing part of old Roman empire

indicators.note: 'in' puts this letter inside what follows
the ruins of a place are its pieces scattered, so the city's letters are rearranged

blocks.note: O is zero, nothing
taken as written

explanation.surface: Nothing is left in the ruins of Naples except a glimpse of the old Roman empire.
explanation.walkthrough: Napoli is the Italian name of Naples.
explanation.definitionFit: Polonia is the Latin name for Poland, a region of the Latin-speaking world Azed links to the old empire.

clue.text: Relish cooking cuts briefly in ovens

indicators.note: cooking transforms ingredients, so the word before it is rearranged
cutting something briefly makes it shorter, so the last letter is dropped

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A chef enjoys cooking cuts of meat quickly in the oven.
explanation.walkthrough: 'cuts' looks like meat, but it is a verb: the shuffled word is cut short.
explanation.definitionFit: A lehr is a long oven in which glass is annealed, cooling slowly after being shaped.

clue.text: The old compensate for fruit pa peeled

indicators.note: peeling removes the outer layer, and 'pa' names the two outside letters that come away

blocks.note: a tropical fruit, also called pawpaw

explanation.surface: Grandfather is to be repaid for fruit he peeled.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The old' marks an archaic word, not old people; the P at the front and A at the end, the 'pa' of the clue, are stripped.
explanation.definitionFit: Apay is an obsolete verb meaning to satisfy or repay, so it fits compensate.

clue.text: Letters regularly delivered by mastiff? I don't believe it! (4, two words)

indicators.note: letters taken at regular intervals come from the word that follows

blocks.note: the second, third, fifth and sixth letters: skip one, take two, repeated

explanation.surface: A postman is amazed when a big dog brings the mail.
explanation.walkthrough: The regular pattern here is skip one, take two, rather than every other letter.
explanation.definitionFit: 'As if!' is an informal retort expressing disbelief or scorn, like 'Yeah, right!'

clue.text: Drive away with van

blocks.note: 'Away!' and 'Go!' are both orders to leave
in tennis, van and ad are both short for advantage

explanation.surface: Driving off in a van.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface pictures a delivery driver; van is the tennis score, not a vehicle.
explanation.definitionFit: To goad is to drive or urge on, as cattle with a pointed stick.

clue.text: Savoury snack — Oz maybe tucks into it

indicators.note: something that tucks into a space goes inside it

blocks.note: it is sex appeal, abbreviated SA
Amos Oz was an Israeli novelist; 'maybe' marks a first name taken from an example

explanation.surface: An Australian tucks hungrily into a savoury pastry.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Oz' looks like Australia, but it is the surname of the writer Amos Oz.
explanation.definitionFit: A samosa is a fried triangular pastry with a spiced filling, a common savoury snack.

clue.text: Impatient to be heard when published, but chary about it

indicators.note: 'about' means around, so the shy word wraps the published one

blocks.note: a book is out once published
chary means wary or shy

explanation.surface: A new author longs for attention once the book is out, yet is wary of it.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone shouty speaks loudly and aggressively, determined to be heard.

clue.text: Elizabeth, queen, completely succeeded for subjects of old

blocks.note: Beth is a short form of Elizabeth
R is short for regina, queen
all means wholly, completely
S is the abbreviation for succeeded in genealogies

explanation.surface: Queen Elizabeth won over her subjects in times past.
explanation.walkthrough: 'subjects' looks like a noun for the queen's people, but it is a verb: enslaves.
explanation.definitionFit: Bethrall is a Spenserian verb meaning to enslave, so 'subjects of old' is its old form.

clue.text: Celebrants, set nervously beset by religious awe repeatedly?

indicators.note: something done nervously is jittery and disordered, so these letters shift
something beset is surrounded on all sides, so it goes inside

blocks.note: taken as written
fear is reverent awe of God; 'repeatedly' makes it plural

explanation.surface: Worshippers at a festival, edgy and overwhelmed by holy dread.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark admits that 'repeatedly' stretches to mean a plural.
explanation.definitionFit: Feasters are people celebrating with a feast, so they are celebrants.

clue.text: Stand? By the sound of it one may be at the end of the line

definitions.text: one may be at the end of the line

indicators.note: this phrase asks you to go by how a word is pronounced rather than written

blocks.note: a dais is a raised platform, a stand, said here as one syllable

blocks.clueFragment: one may be at the end of the line
blocks.note: a fish hooked on an angler's line

explanation.surface: A question about where to stand, and who ends up last in a queue.
explanation.walkthrough: Chambers allows dais to be said as one syllable, rhyming with face. 'end of the line' suggests a queue or a railway terminus, but the line is a fishing line.
explanation.definitionFit: The dace is a small freshwater fish of the carp family, one an angler may catch.
